title: A company knew its waste was poisoning an entire town — and kept dumping for 9 more years.
description:
Cats were dancing in the streets of Minamata. Then they threw themselves into the sea. May 1, 1956. A six-year-old girl arrives at the local hospital — unable to walk, unable to speak, convulsing. Within weeks, dozens more. Cats, birds, fish — all going mad, all dying. Locals call it the strange disease. Nobody knows what causes it. By 1957, researchers trace the pattern to Minamata Bay.

The water glows at night. Chisso Corporation's chemical factory has been dumping methylmercury into the bay since 1932. The mercury concentrates in shellfish and fish. The fish feed the town. Here's what Chisso knew. In 1959, their own chief researcher, Hajime Hosokawa, fed factory wastewater to lab cats. They developed identical symptoms within months. He reported the results to management. Chisso shut down the experiment, locked the files away, and told the public the cause was still unknown. They kept dumping.

For nine more years. The government didn't officially acknowledge the cause until September 1968 — twelve years after the first patients appeared. By then, dozens had died. Thousands were already contaminated. Hosokawa broke his silence in 1970, testifying from his hospital bed. He died weeks later. Chisso never faced criminal charges. Over 2,000 victims were eventually certified. But tens of thousands more who applied were rejected by criteria so narrow most couldn't qualify. The true number will never be known.
